..
Issued at 142 AM CST Sun Nov 15 2026

A negatively tilted trough axis continues to dig across the southern 
Plains toward the Gulf region, driving a stronger surface cyclone 
toward the Mississippi Delta. For the Central Plains and lower 
Missouri River Valley, this has forced a mid-level ridge axis across 
the area, with strong dAVA developing a broad surface anticyclone 
centered along the Middle and Upper portions of the Mississippi 
River Valley. This will continue to push eastward this afternoon, 
and force lower tropospheric flow southeasterly by the afternoon. 
This flow will help boost temperatures this afternoon back into the 
lower and mid 50s across much of the area. Lingering moisture from 
the southern Plains system is currently (as of 07z analysis) over 
western Kansas, and as this trough axis shifts eastward should 
expect to see some high-level cloud cover move in through the 
afternoon and evening. This cloud cover though should clear with 
another push of dAVA and subsidence, eventually clearing skies and 
pushing the moisture southeastward. As a result, clear skies and 
light winds will provide another setup for efficient radiational 
cooling heading into Monday morning, sending low temperatures into 
the lower 30s for most of the forecast area,  with some upper 20s 
possible near the Iowa state line. 

Monday morning and afternoon, dAVA regime remains in place tracking 
a broad surface anticyclone across the Central Great Lakes region 
and Ohio River Valley. This will turn low-level flow across eastern 
Kansas to Central Missouri southerly, with stronger WAA between 
925mb-850mb. There should be enough mixing Monday afternoon to help 
get temperatures back toward the upper 50s for most of the area, and 
perhaps some lower 60s for areas south of U.S. Hwy. 50. If skies 
remain clear Monday night, we may see a strong diurnal cycle once 
again where lows drop into the lower 30s Tuesday morning, especially 
for areas east of Interstate 35, though uncertainty is a bit higher 
amongst ensemble members, with probabilities of dropping below 35F 
are only around 20 percent. Tuesday and Wednesday, continued 
southerly flow and push of the thermal ridge axis into the eastern 
Plains will continue to send temperatures upward, reaching the lower 
to mid 60s by Wednesday afternoon. Through the middle of the work 
week, overnight and early morning lows should mostly be above 40F, 
and perhaps some spots may only drop into the lower 50s. The 
forecast remains mostly dry through the middle of the week.

The ridge axis is progged to be completely east of the area by 
Wednesday afternoon or evening. Deterministic guidance depicts a 
short-wave trough lifting northeastward into the Northern Plains and 
Upper Midwest, dragging a surface cyclone along that path. The bulk 
of the forcing looks to remain well north of the area on Thursday, 
though subtle surface pressure falls may be able to reach the lower 
Missouri River Valley. With the exiting surface anticyclone though, 
flow becomes more southwesterly, bringing in drier air ahead of the 
axis of convergence from the northern Plains cyclone. Ensembles are 
depicting about 15-20 percent probabilities for some type of rainfall 
on Thursday afternoon or evening, but will be battling a lot of dry 
air. Continued WAA and favorable regimes for mixing may help 
temperatures Thursday and Friday reach the lower 70s south of U.S. 
Hwy. 50, with mid to upper 60s elsewhere across the area. 

Next weekend, a stronger H5 trough and notable vort maxima is 
depicted in our extended guidance, that brings stronger mid-level 
forcing and a surface cyclone closer to the area, with an attendant 
cold front pushing across the Plains. This will introduce higher 
rainfall chances, between 50-60 percent across most of the forecast 
area. With the notable warmup, all precipitation will be rain. While 
the forcing could end up quite strong on Saturday, the placement of 
theta-e advection may be removed from our area during peak diurnal 
heating. As a result, current extended guidance depicts minimal CAPE 
and instability developing in our area, which could largely limit 
the threat for thunderstorms. Trends will need to continued to be 
monitored, because changes in the propagation speed of the wave could 
result in a different placement of a CAPE axis that could make 
Saturday more active. Once this system passes, seasonable 
temperatures are forecast by the end of next weekend.
